candidates.description: I hope they find peace soon. 😭 Till then… do you think I should do a whole series covering more of these epsilon–delta proofs? 👀 Because even with all this fun context, epsilon and delta are genuinely a mathematician’s best friends. 💛 Why? Because they give us a precise language to talk about ideas that otherwise feel almost impossible to pin down. Take a limit. We casually say, “as x gets closer and closer to a, f(x) gets closer and closer to L.” But what does “closer and closer” actually mean? How close is close enough? How do we quantify that closeness? And how can we turn an intuitive statement into something we can actually prove? That’s where ε (epsilon) and δ (delta) enter. For every tiny tolerance ε that we choose for the output, we can find a corresponding δ that tells us how close x needs to be to a. And suddenly, this vague idea of “approaching” becomes a mathematically precise statement. That is the beauty of the epsilon–delta definition of a limit — it teaches us how mathematics turns intuition into rigor. And honestly… this is one of the moments where calculus starts becoming real analysis. 🥹 So yes, epsilon and delta may be having their own little marital crisis here… …but mathematically? Best friends. candidates.title: these spinning circles are drawing a dotted sixteenth note 🎵
candidates.description: The outline of a dotted sixteenth note, sampled at 2048 points, is a sum of spinning circles: z(t) = ∑ cₖ eⁱᵏᵗ, with the cₖ from its discrete Fourier transform. Circle k has radius |cₖ| and turns k times per lap. Keep only the N biggest circles and the widest gap to the outline is 27.9% of the symbol's height at N = 2, 9.0% at N = 8, 2.7% at N = 32, 0.58% at N = 128 and 0.14% at N = 512. The dot is a separate shape, so the circles draw the note as one continuous line and hop across to the dot and back: the short straight stroke near the notehead is that hop. The sound is built the same way: an A that gains overtones every time more circles join, with more plucked notes each stage. You asked for a dotted sixteenth (and a semiquaver) in the comments, so here it is. candidates.title: Why 0.999... Is Mathematically Equal to 1
candidates.description: 0.999... is not "almost 1" — it is literally another way of writing the exact number 1. This 10-second visual explainer breaks down why the repeating decimal 0.999... equals 1 using a single 1×1 unit square and four classic mathematical proofs: The Fraction Proof: 1/3 = 0.333..., so multiplying both sides by 3 gives 3/3 = 0.999... = 1. The Algebraic Proof: Setting x = 0.999... and subtracting it from 10x = 9.999... leaves 9x = 9, so x = 1. The Infinite Geometric Series: Adding 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... fills the entire unit square with zero leftover space. The Number Line: Between any two distinct real numbers, you can always fit another number. Because 1 − 0.999... = 0, no number exists between them. Key insight: Our intuition trips up because we expect every real number to have only one decimal representation. In reality, any terminating decimal (like 1 or 0.5) can also be written as an infinite repeating 9s decimal (0.999... or 0.4999...). Save this Short as a quick reference for calculus, real analysis, or the next time this math debate comes up. #Mathematics #0999Equals1 #MathExplained

candidates.title: “Israel and Palestine: The Short History Explained
candidates.description: Why have Israelis and Palestinians been in conflict for so long? Here’s the short version. Both groups have deep ties to the same land. In the early 1900s, the area was ruled by the Ottoman Empire, and then by Britain after World War 1. Arab people had lived there for generations, and a growing number of Jewish people were arriving, many hoping for a safe homeland after facing persecution in Europe. In 1947, the United Nations proposed splitting the land into a Jewish state and an Arab state. Jewish leaders accepted the plan, and Arab leaders rejected it. In 1948, Israel declared independence, and a war followed with neighboring Arab countries. Israelis remember it as their war of independence. Palestinians call it the “Nakba,” meaning catastrophe, because hundreds of thousands of Palestinians left or were forced from their homes. In 1967, another war left Israel in control of the West Bank, Gaza, and East Jerusalem. Since then, the main disagreements have been about borders, security, Jerusalem, and refugees. Many peace efforts have been tried, including the Oslo Accords in 1993, but a lasting agreement hasn’t been reached. Both peoples have suffered, and both want a safe home. Each rectangle represents an approximate contribution to the total area, and the sum of these individual areas provides an estimate of the definite integral. As the number of rectangles increases, the width of each rectangle decreases, producing a more accurate approximation of the actual area. This mathematical visualization illustrates the fundamental relationship between finite sums, limits, and calculus. Watch how the number of rectangles increases progressively, making the rectangular approximation approach the smooth region beneath the sine curve. The comparison between the numerical Riemann sum and the exact value of the definite integral highlights one of the most important ideas in mathematical analysis. The definite integral of sin(x) over the interval from zero to pi equals 2. This result provides a clear example of how integration calculates the accumulated area under a function and how numerical approximation methods can approach an exact mathematical result. The visualization also introduces the midpoint Riemann sum, a numerical integration technique that uses the midpoint of each subinterval to determine the height of its corresponding rectangle. This video is ideal for students learning calculus, definite integrals, limits, numerical integration, and the mathematical foundations of area calculation. It helps make abstract mathematical concepts more intuitive by connecting graphical representations with numerical approximations and analytical results. Key mathematical concepts explored in this video include Riemann sums, definite integration, the sine function, area under a curve, midpoint approximation, limits, continuous functions, and the relationship between summation and integration. These concepts form an essential foundation for advanced calculus, mathematical modeling, physics, engineering, numerical analysis, and other scientific applications. For students preparing for mathematics examinations, competitive exams, or higher-level calculus courses, this visual explanation offers an accessible way to understand how integration emerges from the process of adding increasingly smaller contributions. Mathematics teachers can also use this example to demonstrate the connection between geometric area, numerical approximation, and exact integration. candidates.description: Your fingers never really touch your phone…#QuantumPhysics #QuantumMechanics #Physics #Science #Mbbs Have you ever wondered whether you truly touch anything? 🤯 According to quantum physics, touching is more complicated than it seems! Atoms contain nuclei surrounded by electron clouds. When your hand approaches a table, electromagnetic interactions between the atoms resist being pushed together. 5 Japanese Phrases for When Something Goes Wrong — and the Numbers to Call
candidates.description: Japan is very safe. These five phrases are the small amount of preparation that stays worth doing anyway. For solo travellers and anyone moving to Japan. Ten seconds of preparation for a situation you will probably never meet. Taught by Saku. ▶ Learn Japanese live, 1-on-1, with a hand-picked teacher: https://kodawari-sensei.com/en?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_content=kt31saku ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🚨 The five やめてください — yamete kudasai — "Stop it!" たすけてください — tasukete kudasai — "Help me!" だいじょうぶです — daijōbu desu — "No, thank you." / "I'm fine." けいさつをよんでください — keisatsu o yonde kudasai — "Call the police." えいごはなせますか？ — eigo hanasemasu ka? — "Do you speak English?" **110** — police · **119** — fire and ambulance. Both free from any phone, including a locked one. **だいじょうぶです is the one you will actually use** — it is how you decline anything in Japan, firmly and without confrontation. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🗾 The small police box on the corner 交番 — こうばん — kōban — a neighbourhood police box 交 — こう — kō — exchange, alternate 番 — ばん — ban — a turn, a watch, a number Literally "alternating watch" — officers took shifts. **There are over 6,000 of them across Japan**, usually a small building at a busy intersection with a red lamp outside, staffed around the clock. **And it is the single most useful thing to know about being lost in Japan.** A 交番 is not a police station — it is closer to a permanently staffed help desk that happens to be police. Officers there will: - give you directions, with a map, at any hour - take lost property. **Japan's lost-and-found rate is genuinely remarkable** and it runs through 交番. - lend you the train fare home in some cases 落とし物 — おとしもの — otoshimono — a lost item 忘れ物 — わすれもの — wasuremono — something left behind 交番はどこですか — kōban wa doko desu ka — where's the police box? **If you lose something on a train**, it goes to the station office first and then to a central lost property centre. Report it — the recovery rate for phones and wallets in Japan is high enough that it is worth the twenty minutes. The bigger buildings: 警察署 — けいさつしょ — keisatsusho — a full police station 派出所 — はしゅつじょ — hashutsujo — the older word for 交番, still on some signs And 番 turns up all over: 交番, 一番 (ichiban, number one), 番号 (bangō, a number), 当番 (tōban, being on duty). 🔎 emergency Japanese phrases, koban police box Japan, 110 119 Japan, lost something in Japan, otoshimono, yamete kudasai, solo travel Japan safety. #Shorts #LearnJapanese #Japanese #JapanTravel #JapanSafety

candidates.title: How trigonmetry measures hidden heights #maths #trigonometry #science#learn#shorts #likeandsubscribe
candidates.description: The first use of the idea of ‘sine’ in the way we use it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata, in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardha-jya for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which means curve, when the Arabic version was translated into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine, became common in mathematical texts throughout Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated notation ‘sin’. The origin of the terms ‘cosine’ and ‘tangent’ was much later. The cosine function arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta called it kotijya. The name cosinus originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation ‘cos’.

candidates.description: Two balls start at the same point and finish at the same point. One rolls down a straight ramp, the shortest path. The other takes a longer curve that even dips below the finish. Which one arrives first? The curve wins by almost a full second. A ball's speed depends only on how far it has dropped, and the curve drops steeply right at the start, so its ball is nearly three times as fast after one second. candidates.title: INELASTIC DEMAND? ⛽📈 Petrol +30%, Use Only -5%! #economics #shorts
candidates.description: Petrol +30%, petrol use only -5%. That is relatively inelastic demand: elasticity between 0 and 1. Steep demand curve, oil import bill, current account deficit, inflation, and why governments tax petrol and cigarettes. Part 5 of the elasticity of demand series. Follow and subscribe for the next part. Transcript: Suppose petrol prices jump thirty percent, but petrol consumption falls only five percent. That is exactly why fuel is every government's favourite tax. Demand is relatively inelastic when the percentage change in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage change in price. Elasticity lies between zero and one. Follow us, this is part five of the elasticity series. On the graph, the demand curve is steep. A big rise in price, from P1 to P2, causes only a small fall in quantity, from Q1 to Q2. The green change in price is much bigger than the red change in quantity. Here, elasticity is five divided by thirty, about zero point one seven. Necessities like fuel, wheat flour and electricity behave this way. So when global oil prices rise, the import bill jumps, the current account deficit widens, and inflation spreads across the economy. It is also why governments tax petrol and cigarettes. Quantity barely falls, so tax revenue rises, and most of the burden falls on consumers. Exam point. When demand is inelastic, a price rise increases total revenue, and a price cut reduces it. Next up, the final type, perfectly inelastic demand. Follow and subscribe to us so you don't miss it. #economics #elasticityofdemand #inelasticdemand #microeconomics #inflation #shorts

Bharata's Padukas | 3 Leadership Lessons from Ramayana for Project Managers #shorts
candidates.description: 🏹 WHAT HAPPENS TO YOUR PROJECT WHEN THE LEADER IS AWAY? Does work continue smoothly—or do important decisions pile up? The story of Bharata's Padukas from the Ramayana offers a powerful lesson about delegation, authority, and responsible leadership. Welcome to Episode 02 of Ramayana × Project Management by PMO Wisdom! 🎯 TODAY'S STORY: BHARATA'S PADUKAS When Rama was in exile, Bharata placed Rama's sandals (Padukas) on the throne and governed in his name for fourteen years. Bharata's actions symbolised his commitment to Rama's rightful authority and his responsibility to serve as a steward. What can project managers learn from this story? ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 1: MAKE AUTHORITY VISIBLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Everyone should know who has the authority to make decisions. In project management, unclear decision rights can create delays, confusion, and unnecessary escalation. Before a planned absence, clarify: ✅ Who can make routine decisions ✅ Which decisions require escalation ✅ What approval limits apply ✅ Who communicates important decisions A project should not stop simply because one person is unavailable. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 2: ACT AS A STEWARD, NOT AN OWNER ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Bharata governed in Rama's name rather than claiming the throne as his own. In project management, delegated authority should be exercised responsibly. A project manager or deputy should: • Respect the sponsor's intent • Work within agreed decision limits • Protect the project's objectives • Remain accountable for decisions made Leadership is about serving the agreed purpose, not treating delegated authority as personal power. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 3: HAND BACK CLEANLY ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Delegation should include a clear process for handing responsibility back. Maintain: ✅ A transparent decision log ✅ Records of important approvals ✅ A list of unresolved issues ✅ Clear communication about changes When the original leader returns, they should be able to understand what happened and resume responsibility without confusion. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 💡 PRACTICAL PROJECT EXAMPLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Imagine a project manager takes three weeks of leave. BEFORE: ❌ 40 decisions are waiting ❌ Nobody knows who can approve what ❌ Progress slows down AFTER: ✅ A deputy is appointed ✅ Decision limits are defined ✅ A decision log is maintained ✅ The project keeps moving The difference is not the absence of the leader. It is the clarity of delegated authority. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ⚠️ MISTAKE TO AVOID ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Leaving a project without clear delegation. When nobody knows who can decide, even small issues may remain unresolved. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🎯 TRY THIS IN YOUR NEXT PROJECT ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Before your next planned absence: 1️⃣ Identify your deputy. 2️⃣ Define their decision-making authority. 3️⃣ Agree on escalation limits. 4️⃣ Establish a decision log and handback process. Ask yourself: "Who covers for me when I'm away?" 💡 KEY TAKEAWAY MAKE AUTHORITY VISIBLE. ACT AS A STEWARD. HAND BACK CLEANLY. Strong governance allows work to continue while preserving accountability. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🎬 RAMAYANA × PROJECT MANAGEMENT ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Episode 02/12 — Bharata's Padukas NEXT EPISODE: Episode 03 — Jatayu's Warning Explore timeless stories from the Ramayana and their practical connections with leadership, project governance, decision-making, and stakeholder management. 📺 Subscribe to PMO Wisdom: https://youtube.com/@PMOWisdom One Topic. candidates.title: Why a Paper Cut Hurts More Than a Knife Cut
candidates.description: How does a harmless sheet of paper slice your finger worse than a kitchen knife, when it's made from 99% water and zero glue? 📄🔪 Here's the full journey: giant spinning blades chop a log into wood chips, a pressure tank boils out the brown natural glue (lignin), and the leftover white fibers become a soup that's 99% water. candidates.description: Is the United Kingdom one country or four? 🇬🇧 The UK has one king, one passport and one army, yet it includes four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each with its own capital. It all started with England, which conquered Wales in the 13th century and surrounded it with massive castles 🏰 The Scots resisted for centuries, until in 1603 their king inherited the English throne and moved to London 👑 Facing financial difficulties, Scotland agreed to a full union in 1707 but kept its own laws, courts and church ⚖️ That’s how Great Britain was formed. Ireland was also conquered by the English but kept its own parliament, until that parliament was bought with titles and money and voted for union. In 1801, the United Kingdom was created 💰 After the Easter Rising and the Irish War of Independence, most of the island broke away and only the north remained ☘️ That’s why its official name is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland: four countries in one sovereign state, but never one nation. #unitedkingdom #uk #greatbritain #britain #england #scotland #wales #northernireland #ireland #britishhistory #ukhistory #history #europeanhistory #london #europe #border #learning #geography #map

Discover the extraordinary art and fascinating lives of Margaret Macdonald and Frances Macdonald, two pioneering female artists who helped shape the Glasgow Style and the Art Nouveau movement at the turn of the 20th century. Often associated with the mysterious Spook School, the Macdonald sisters created some of the most distinctive, dreamlike, and symbolically rich works of modern decorative art. In this art history documentary, we explore the lives, artistic influences, and remarkable contributions of Margaret and Frances Macdonald, members of the legendary Glasgow Four alongside Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Herbert MacNair. Together, they developed a revolutionary visual language combining Art Nouveau design, Symbolism, spirituality, nature, and the Arts and Crafts movement. Learn how the Glasgow School of Art became the center of an artistic revolution, and how the Macdonald sisters transformed traditional ideas about beauty, femininity, and decorative art. Explore their connections to Japanese art and Japonisme, Celtic knotwork, Symbolist painting, and the flowing organic lines of Art Nouveau. We examine the distinctive characteristics of the Glasgow Style, including elongated ethereal figures, flowing hair, mysterious dreamlike compositions, intricate decorative patterns, symbolic flowers, and delicate pastel colors. Their innovative use of watercolor, gouache, gesso, metallic paint, glass beads, and mother-of-pearl created extraordinary textured surfaces that blurred the boundaries between fine art, interior design, and decorative arts. Famous Artworks Explored in This Video Frances Macdonald – A Paradox (1895): An unsettling Symbolist composition exploring duality, mystery, and the themes of life and death. Margaret Macdonald – The May Queen (1900): An exquisite decorative work celebrating spring, renewal, femininity, and nature. Margaret Macdonald – The White Rose and the Red Rose (1902): A symbolic composition exploring romantic love, purity, spirituality, and the beauty of Art Nouveau design. Frances Macdonald – The Choice (c. 1896): A psychologically intense watercolor exploring spiritual choices, temptation, and opposing forces. Discover why the sisters' work initially confused and shocked London critics, earning the nickname the Spook School, while attracting admiration from the Vienna Secession and influential artists such as Gustav Klimt. We also examine how their artistic legacy extended beyond Art Nouveau, influencing modern decorative design, Art Deco, Symbolism, and even later movements exploring dreams, fantasy, and the subconscious, including Surrealism. For many years, the achievements of Margaret and Frances Macdonald were overshadowed by their husbands, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Herbert MacNair. Today, their work is increasingly recognized for its originality, innovation, and profound contribution to modern art. Explore the fascinating world of the Glasgow Four, Art Nouveau, Symbolism, and the visionary women artists who helped redefine modern art. candidates.title: Why the first second always feels longer #science #neuroscience #explained
candidates.description: Look at a clock with a second hand. That first second always seems to hang there a beat too long. 👁️ Getting your eyes to the clock takes a saccade — a fast jump — and your brain turns the picture down while your eyes are moving. That leaves a gap of missing footage. 🕐 Rather than show you the gap, your brain backdates the first thing you land on and fills the missing interval with it. So the stretched second isn't your imagination: you really were shown that image for longer than a second. ⏱️ It's called chronostasis, and the stretch is small — measurements put it at up to roughly a tenth of a second — but it's reliable enough that you can trigger it on purpose with any clock. 👀 It's also the same suppression that makes it impossible to watch your own eyes move in a mirror. One hides a movement; the other stretches a moment. There's a separate video on this channel about the mirror version. 🔔 Subscribe for more short explainers on why your body does the weird things it does. #science #humanbody #shorts

Behavioral Neuroscience
candidates.description: Cognitive neuroscience studies thoughts. Behavioral neuroscience studies what you actually do. Here is what the research actually says about behavioral neuroscience. It is the biological basis of behaviour, in humans and in animals, and it grew out of what used to be called physiological psychology. Every study has the same skeleton: measure activity somewhere in the nervous system, then set it against one behavioural variable. A perception, a reaction, a decision. The thought in between belongs to the other field. KEY FACTS - Behavioral neuroscience is the study of the biological basis of behavior in humans and animals. - It is the broader, contemporary development of Physiological Psychology and is sometimes called Biological Psychology. - It examines the brain's neurotransmissions and the psychological events associated with biological activity. - Topics span genetic and molecular substrates of behavior, neuropsychology, learning and memory, motivation and emotion, and sensory processes. - The field studies the interplay between the brain, behavior and the environment. - Studies examine what creates, controls and coordinates perception, action, reaction or decision-making. Read the full behavioral neuroscience article: https://www.emotiv.com/blogs/glossary/behavioral-neuroscience EMOTIV translates peer-reviewed neuroscience into short, accurate explainers. No hype. Every claim in this video comes from the sources listed above. #brain #memory #focus

candidates.description: Did you know that humans learned to make bread nearly 4,000 years before the invention of agriculture? The world's oldest known bread-like remains date back approximately **14,400 years!** In this fascinating historical documentary, discover how prehistoric humans made the first bread without farming, modern ovens, or cooking utensils. Around 14,400 years ago, ancient hunter-gatherers collected wild wheat (Einkorn), wild barley, and edible plant roots. Archaeological discoveries at Shubayqa 1 in Jordan revealed charred bread-like food remains, providing remarkable evidence of food preparation before agriculture. candidates.title: Camo doesn't look like a forest. On purpose. But why?
candidates.description: Look at a pair of camo pants: green, brown and black blobs with hard edges. They don't look like leaves or bark. Nothing in a forest looks like that, yet in the woods they can make you nearly impossible to spot. Camo was born in the sky. In World War One, the airplane let the enemy look straight down at your lines, and a cannon spotted from above could be destroyed by artillery. In September 1914, a French gunner named Lucien-Victor Guirand de Scévola, who had painted soft pastels before the war, hid a gun under a canvas painted to blend in with the ground. In February 1915 the French army set up its first camouflage unit. By the end of the year Scévola was running it, and he filled it with artists, including Cubists. Your eye doesn't really find a gun by its color. It finds it by its outline. Paint a cannon the perfect green and from the air it's still a cannon. Cover it in clashing patches that run across its edges, and the eye stops seeing one shape. It sees pieces. Picasso saw it right away. In February 1915 he wrote to a friend in the artillery suggesting the guns be painted in bright bits of red, yellow, green, blue and white, like a harlequin. Walking through Paris with Gertrude Stein, he watched one of the first camouflaged cannons roll past and said, "We made that." He never painted a gun, but Scévola said almost the same thing: to completely change what an object looked like, he had to use the methods the Cubists used to paint it. Soon the painters were hiding everything. In 1917 the British painter Norman Wilkinson covered ships in wild stripes and zigzags, so a submarine captain looking through his periscope couldn't tell which way a ship was heading, or how fast. More than 4,000 British ships were painted that way. It was called dazzle. It took more than ten years for camo to be printed on cloth. One of the first patterns, Germany's splinter camo of 1931, looks like it came straight out of a Cubist painting.

candidates.title: What happens when you add 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 forever? #maths #shorts #science  #3blue1brown
candidates.description: An infinite series can converge to a finite sum, even when you keep adding positive numbers forever. By slicing a single square into smaller fractions, we can visualize how adding 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and beyond fills the total area of 1 exactly. This geometric approach shows that as long as each new piece covers only half of the remaining space, the total area will never exceed the boundaries of the original square. Understanding how an infinite series works helps clarify why these sums do not explode to infinity. Seeing the math as a physical shape makes the concept of convergence intuitive, proving that a finite sum is the logical result of this process. How Italy Became One Country, From 7 Pieces to 1 Kingdom 🤯  #geography #animation #history #shorts
candidates.description: In 1859 there was no country called Italy. The peninsula was split into seven pieces: kingdoms, duchies, the Papal States, and Austrian-ruled Lombardy and Venetia. Just twelve years later, Rome was the capital of a united Kingdom of Italy. Here's how it happened: Sardinia teamed up with France in 1859, central Italy voted to join in 1860, Garibaldi's Thousand took the south, the Kingdom of Italy was born on 17 March 1861, Venice followed in 1866, and Rome in 1870. Italy as a state is younger than the USA (1861 vs 1776), but Italian history and culture go back thousands of years. candidates.title: NASA Found a Tiny Moon Hiding in Saturn’s Rings! 😳🪐 #Shorts
candidates.description: Scientists spotted mysterious waves in Saturn’s rings before discovering the tiny moon responsible for them! 😳🪐 Meet Daphnis, one of Saturn’s smallest and most fascinating moons! Approximately 8 kilometers (5 miles) across, Daphnis orbits inside the 42-kilometer-wide Keeler Gap in Saturn’s A ring. But here's what makes this discovery incredible: Before Daphnis was discovered on May 1, 2005, scientists had already suspected a hidden moon was there because of mysterious ripples along the edge of the Keeler Gap! Its gravity creates waves in the surrounding ring particles, sculpting the edges of the gap. These waves extend both horizontally and vertically, creating incredible structures in Saturn’s rings. NASA’s Cassini spacecraft captured its closest-ever view of Daphnis on January 16, 2017. Even a tiny moon can reshape the rings of a giant planet! 🔭 NASA Official Sources: Daphnis – NASA: https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/daphnis/ 🌌 Follow Qunova Labs for fascinating space discoveries, astronomy facts, NASA discoveries and mysteries of our universe. #saturn #daphnis #nasa #saturnrings #space #astronomy #spacefacts #science #spaceexploration #shorts

candidates.title: This sun is no brighter than the sky around it | Impression, Sunrise #art #history
candidates.description: Fine art films for art lovers, museumgoers and anyone who hangs art at home. The short ones find the detail most people miss in a famous painting; the long ones pair paintings with classical music for reading, studying or a quiet evening. Claude Monet painted the harbour of Le Havre at sunrise in 1872, and the picture gave Impressionism its name. The orange sun looks like the brightest thing on the canvas, but when its brightness is measured, it is the same as the grey sky around it. Take the colour away and the sun almost disappears. Harvard neuroscientist Margaret Livingstone explains why it seems to shimmer: the part of our vision that judges position and depth sees only brightness, not colour, so it can't pin the sun down. The painting hangs in the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris. There's a new painting every day, so subscribe if you'd like to keep looking. candidates.description: How are computers in a network connected?
